item.title: Source-Aware Dynamic Pricing with Strategic Buyers
item.description: arXiv:2610.22516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In modern commerce, firms and platforms typically use customer features from different sources to personalize prices: some features are verified using seller records or third-party data, while others are self-reported and may be strategically manipulated by buyers seeking lower prices. We therefore introduce a novel source-aware framework for contextual dynamic pricing with strategic buyers in a high-dimensional semiparametric setting, where buyer valuations follow a sparse linear model with an unknown noise distribution. To account for differences in manipulability across feature sources while enabling effective valuation learning, we develop the Source-Aware Localized exploration and calibrated Exploitation (SALE) pricing policy, which draws on verified features to localize price exploration and combines verified and reported features to correct for strategic manipulation during exploitation. Our localized exploration design allows converting binary purchase feedback into unbiased signals of conditional mean valuations, yielding a new population equation that supports consistent sparse estimation despite non-i.i.d. buyer arrivals. Building on this estimate, we develop a localized empirical-process analysis that exploits intrinsic sparse geometry to establish uniform guarantees for nonparametric estimation of the noise distribution in the high-dimensional setting. With these estimation guarantees, we establish SALE's self-recovery property, which keeps localized exploration valid with high probability and leads to a sublinear expected regret bound. Both simulation studies and real-data experiments demonstrate the appealing performance of SALE. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to provide a theoretical and practical framework for incorporating information provenance into dynamic pricing with strategic buyers.
item.dc:creator: Jinjiang Zou, Yang Li, Zemin Zheng

item.title: Is a Linear Probe Evidence of a Linear Representation?
item.description: arXiv:2610.22655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The linear representation hypothesis holds that pretrained vision models encode generative factors as linearly decodable directions in feature space, and comes with a standard methodology: train a linear probe, declare a factor represented if accuracy is high. We show this test is too permissive. Asymptotically, any sufficiently rich feature map, including a random one, admits a linear readout, so high probe accuracy is consistent with two very different geometries: a true linear world model, where the latent-aligned subspace dominates the representation, or a kernel machine, where the latents lie linearly inside a much larger curved manifold. This distinction matters because the curved structure orthogonal to the probe is relevant for out-of-distribution generalization, robustness, and compositional transfer. We propose three asymmetric diagnostics that distinguish the two cases: reverse predictivity, spectral concentration, and out-of-distribution generalization. We validate them in a fully observed simulation where ground truth is known. Applied to six pretrained vision transformers on SVG-World, our deterministic generative benchmark with paired visual styles, and to two of them on CelebA, they show pretraining produces structure beyond a random kernel but well short of a linear world model. On dSprites, 3D Shapes and MPI3D, forward decodability and latent-aligned variance dissociate. Thus, forward decoding alone does not show that the probed factors align with the dominant geometry of the representation. In summary, our work cautions about the success of linear probes as opposed to truly linear and low dimensional representations.
item.dc:creator: Nadir Kutluozen, Christian Intern\`o, David Klindt

item.title: Optimal approximation of smooth functions by ReLU neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.22693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study uniform approximation of the H\"older ball $\mathcal H_1^s([0,1]^D)$ by fully connected ReLU networks. Except in the one-dimensional Lipschitz case, existing constructions remain separated from the information-theoretic efficiency limit. This article closes the gap for every $s>0$ and $D\ge1$: networks with width $O(N)$, depth $O(L)$, and parameter magnitude $O(1)$ attain uniform approximation error of order $(N^2L^2\log N)^{-s/D}$. No relation between width and depth is required. The construction uses new encoding and decoding mechanisms that exploit higher-order finite-difference bounds for local Taylor coefficients of the target function. As a statistical consequence, empirical risk minimizers over the corresponding clipped network classes attain the minimax regression rate $n^{-2s/(2s+D)}$ without additional logarithmic factors. The paper also gives a detailed exposition of the key approximation techniques, covering both established and new mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Nagler

item.title: Unit-level aggregation breaks coverage in causal foundation models
item.description: arXiv:2610.22770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal foundation models (CFMs) show promising results for treatment-effect estimation, with unit-level estimates that are competitive on standard benchmarks. Many causal analyses, however, inform decisions through effects averaged over groups of units, such as the full sample, the treated units, or a subgroup, and for such decisions a CFM is useful only if its credible intervals are calibrated. We examine these intervals and find that their coverage degrades, both in simple synthetic settings and on standard benchmarks. On ACIC 2016, for example, temperature-calibrated 95% intervals from CausalPFN fall below nominal coverage beyond groups of 30 out of 4802 units, and intervals for the full-sample average contain the true value in only 20% of datasets. We trace this problem to how these models are trained and how their intervals are formed. They output a predictive distribution for one unit at a time and, at inference time, combine the unit-level variances as if the errors on different units were independent. We show formally that posterior uncertainty over the data-generating process makes these errors correlated. As a result, the combined variance is too small by a factor that grows with the size of the group. Empirically, this factor predicts where coverage fails and by how much. We then show that two neural process models, which make joint predictions for a group of units, account for this correlation and substantially improve coverage on synthetic tasks and, as heads on a frozen CausalPFN, on all six benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Gabe Schulman, Lucius E. J. Bynum, Yoav Wald

item.title: Distinguishability and Recovery for a Doubly Sparse Spiked Wigner Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.23033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study distinguishability and recovery of a sparse rank-one signal in a spiked Wigner model with independently sparse noise through a variety of algorithms and parameter regimes. The signal and noise have separate sparsity parameters, while the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) remains of constant order as the matrix size grows. For sub-Gaussian noise and spikes whose nonzero coordinates are bounded away from zero, a leave-one-out quadratic thresholding procedure (a generalization of Ding et al., 2024) identifies the support. Sign synchronization yields exact recovery for a Rademacher spike, and spectral refinement yields strong recovery. The quadratic thresholding search parameter gives an explicit tradeoff between signal sparsity, noise sparsity, and computational cost. We also study extensions to sub-Gaussian spike priors through diagonal and quadratic thresholding. For Rademacher spikes with continuous nonzero noise, we develop an identical search algorithm that exploits unblurred signal entries, the existence of which permits distinguishability; connectivity of the graph they reveal provides a sufficient condition for exact recovery. These guarantees do not require moment assumptions on the continuous noise distribution. Together with our previous PCA results (Dumitriu et al., 2026), our analysis covers almost the entire space of parameters and regimes for distinguishing and recovering in our doubly sparse spiked Wigner model.
item.dc:creator: Ioana Dumitriu, JD Flynn, Zhichao Wang

item.title: Information-Geometric Blind Spots of Conformal Test Martingales
item.description: arXiv:2610.23131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conformal test martingales (CTMs) are e-processes for sequentially testing exchangeability via p-values produced by a conformity function $A$. However, any distribution shift that preserves the push-forward $P\circ A^{-1}$ leaves the p-value distribution invariant, rendering it invisible to every CTM based on $A$. We formalise this blind spot through the \emph{$A$-equivalence class} $[P]_A$ and show that, for any target distribution $T$, there is a unique closest element $Q^\ast\in[P]_A$ in KL divergence---the \emph{$A$-cryptic I-projection}---with explicit density $q^\ast(z) = t(z)\,p_S(A(z))/t_S(A(z))$ and a Pythagorean decomposition into detectable and cryptic components. When $A$ is the Neyman-Pearson likelihood ratio, the cryptic component vanishes, connecting our result to optimal e-value design. We demonstrate the theory on high-dimensional image data by empirically constructing this I-projection. By conditionally resampling EMNIST letters to identically match the conformity scores of MNIST digits, we demonstrate that a distribution can be shifted to a disjoint support while leaving the test martingale mathematically blinded.
item.dc:creator: Johan Hallberg Szabadv\'ary

item.title: The Loss or the Architecture? What Matters in Survival Analysis with Competing Risks
item.description: arXiv:2610.23322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Often, \emph{eg} in healthcare and predictive maintenance, what matters is which of several competing causes will strike first, and with what probability: survival analysis with competing risks. Corresponding deep learning methods are developed as bundles: a new architecture together with a new training loss, tested on one to five datasets against a handful of baselines. Thus, a state-of-the-art result cannot be attributed to the architecture, the loss, or the evaluation protocol. The coupling is not accidental: with one incidence curve per cause, a network's head is tied to the losses expressible on it. We vary the two axes independently, three losses, two of them strictly proper, on four backbones, across two modalities that tease the axes apart: 20 tabular and 3 pathology-image datasets. One loss wins in both: modelling cumulative incidence directly under censoring weighting. It brings twice as much as benefits a good choice of backbone on competing-risks data, and no more than it on single-event data: the loss is decisive for competing risks. The backbone matters too, and must match the modality: tabular networks lead on tables, pretrained vision encoders on images. The two choices compound rather than substitute. Proper scoring rules reveal these dynamics; the concordance index (C-index), which is not proper, does not separate models: neither axis moves it, not even tuning on the loss built to improve it. This is an avenue of progress: composed, the two give a model nobody has tried, RealMLP or TabM trained with the cumulative-incidence loss, which takes the best Brier score in our benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Julie Alberge, Ga\"el Varoquaux, Judith Ab\'ecassis

item.title: Towards optimal selection schedules for online active learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.23477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of online linear classification, where a stream of unlabeled samples is available, and annotation is costly. We investigate the optimal query policy, that prescribes whether and when a sample should be labeled and used for a training step, or instead discarded, so as to minimize a given objective. We focus on the realizable case, under Gaussian design, in the high-dimensional regime where data dimension and number of unlabeled samples grow proportionally. We consider two objectives: 1) the generalization error under a labeling budget, and 2) a cumulative cost function where mistakes have unit cost and queries cost $\Delta$. We first show that the myopic policies that greedily minimize at all times the increment in the objective correspond to either small or intermediate-margin policies, that prescribe the selection of samples whose margins fall within certain intervals that shrink with time. Within this class, we numerically ascertain the optimal schedules for the selection thresholds that minimize the final values of the objectives. Taking inspiration from the myopic policy for the cumulative cost, we design a very simple query policy schedule that we compare to other proposed heuristics, on synthetic data and real medical image datasets. Finally, we discuss myopic policies for two-layer neural networks, and exemplify how naive margin-based policies can cease to be optimal.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Cui, Francesca Mignacco, Francesco Mori

item.title: Adaptive conformal prediction on the Grassmannian
item.description: arXiv:2610.23508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a conformal prediction framework for regression with Grassmann-valued responses. The proposed method constructs prediction regions in the form of metric balls directly on the Grassmann manifold, using basis-invariant geometric distances as non-conformity measures and scaling the corresponding non-conformity scores through a learned prediction difficulty estimator. This yields locally adaptive, input-dependent prediction regions that respect the underlying manifold geometry, while retaining the finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction under exchangeability. We evaluate several Grassmannian distance metrics and compare their prediction-region efficiency on synthetic benchmarks and an airfoil inverse shape-design problem. The results highlight the advantages of geometry-aware non-conformity scores, while local adaptation improves empirical coverage uniformity across prediction difficulty levels and, in strongly heteroscedastic settings, can substantially reduce prediction-region size while maintaining the target coverage.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Loukrezis, Zachary J. Grey, Dimitris G. Giovanis

item.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.23570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent work has constructed anytime-valid envelopes that do, but deterministic envelopes are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each coupling a specific algorithm to a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for constructing such anytime-valid data-adaptive boundaries for a large class of iterative algorithms. Performance measures of many of these algorithms satisfy a one-step recursion that reduces the entire error analysis to a single general requirement: time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. We formalize this through a strongly adapted sub-$\psi$ condition, and derive off-the-shelf boundary constructions via continuous and discrete mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. We show how these boundaries can be directly coupled with a separate algorithmic analysis that derives the one-step recursion to provide a class of readymade anytime-valid envelopes across diverse settings including stochastic gradient descent (SGD), temporal difference learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD. In particular, for SGD, our framework either recovers or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Soham Bonnerjee, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.23779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how stochastic gradient descent learns internal representations in wide neural networks trained on rich target functions is a central problem in machine learning. We study this question in two-layer neural networks learning target functions represented by networks of the same architecture, with arbitrary nonlinearity, and with network width and input dimension growing proportionally. In this regime, standard approaches for describing the learning dynamics require tracking a diverging number of overlaps, which measure correlations between learned and target features, leaving no obvious description in terms of a few order parameters. Here, we develop a mesoscopic description of learning by characterizing the distribution of overlaps. In the early stages of learning, we find that a Gaussian description of overlap statistics reduces the learning dynamics to a few collective variables that track learning of the target function's linear and quadratic components. We then estimate the timescale of specialization, when Gaussian closure breaks down and individual learned features begin to strongly correlate with specific target features. We find that specialization in extensive-rank networks is accelerated via a quadratic shielding mechanism, whereby learning the linear and quadratic components of the target function filters gradient fluctuations. We finally describe how the activation function determines the pattern of specialization and characterize the subsequent refinement of learned features. Together, these results show how collective learning gives way to individual feature discovery and clarify when learning in large neural networks admits a simple statistical description.
item.dc:creator: Shu Zhou, Jean Barbier, Sebastian Goldt

item.title: Parametric Resonance in Primal-Dual Learning for Slowly Non-Stationary Constrained MDPs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Primal-dual methods for constrained Markov decision processes are analyzed under a two-timescale assumption, with non-stationarity entering through two channels. In the additive channel, where the constraint level oscillates, the dual oscillation saturates at a floor set by the moving optimum and is amplified linearly by the timescale ratio. In the parametric channel, where the constraint sensitivity oscillates, a coherent modulation carries no resonant forcing at any depth: the dual update's stiffness modulation cancels the primal update's damping modulation. Instability instead comes from a mismatch between the constraint estimate used by the primal update and the measurement used by the dual update, producing a parametric resonance at twice the pair's natural frequency. The tolerated mismatch grows with the square root of the forcing bandwidth and collapses with the square root of the dual-to-primal step-size ratio. These results hold on the tangent linear-quadratic reduction around an active saddle, for one constraint and for $K$ constraints under a common modulation and an isotropy condition. Driving both updates from the same estimate removes the resonant forcing but introduces a stationary offset equal to the estimator's bias. In a Lagrangian soft actor-critic agent, the multiplier locks onto the sub-harmonic at the timescale ratios its identified linear loop predicts and a coherent cost critic suppresses the lock-in, while a proportional (PID) term, predicted to leave the lock-in in place, suppresses most of it through the projection of the multiplier.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Baelde

item.title: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for R\'{e}nyi differential privacy
item.description: arXiv:2610.23798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: R\`enyi differential privacy, based on R\`enyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, R\`enyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, R\`enyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in R\`enyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Here we use kernel Stein discrepancies based on escort distributions to provide certificates for R\`enyi differential privacy. By designing the kernel to focus on the relevant privacy directions, we also derive task-aware privacy certificates. We provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and bounds for exponential mechanisms, with separate task-aware guarantees. A real data set example illustrates how the protected comparison set and the released subspace jointly determine the resulting certificates.
item.dc:creator: Leoni Carla Wirth, Tara Trautwein, Gesine Reinert

item.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
item.description: arXiv:2610.23821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Williamson, Niall Jeffrey, Lorne Whiteway

item.title: ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-Matched References for Amortized Simulation-Based Model Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.23825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The evidence, $\mathcal{Z} = p(x | \mathcal{M})$, of a data-generating model $\mathcal{M}$ is a powerful tool in Bayesian frameworks: it enables model inference, model misspecification tests, and goodness-of-fit assessment as an alternative to standard discrepancy statistics, e.g. $\chi^2$. While versatile, the evidence is notoriously difficult to compute, even when the likelihood is available. In both likelihood-based and simulation-based inference, estimating $\mathcal{Z}$ provides an immediate solution to high-dimensional goodness-of-fit or model misspecification tests: using $\mathcal{Z}(x)$ as the test statistic induces a minimum-volume level-$\alpha$ test. Such tests are essential to assess model fidelity, which is necessary to trust simulation-based parameter inference. Existing learned approaches largely target Bayes factors, which only measure evidence ratios. Instead, we provide accurate, fast, and amortized estimates of the absolute evidence. We present ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-matched References. Building on the Evidence Network framework of Jeffrey & Wandelt (2024), the proposed method first learns Bayes factors with respect to a flow-matched reference, from which the absolute evidence is recovered. We show improvement in estimation of $\mathcal{Z}$ over the flow-based baseline in all applications considered and the best performance of all density estimation methods considered in our benchmarks. We furthermore introduce and provide the proof for an architecture that jointly learns the individual evidences of a set of models $\{\mathcal{M}_i\}$. We demonstrate the performance and scaling behavior of these approaches on data from a variety of scientific applications.
item.dc:creator: Kai Lehman, Jameson Dong, Carolina Cuesta-Lazaro, Niall Jeffrey, Benjamin D. Wandelt, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Sven Krippendorf, Jochen Weller

item.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO
item.description: arXiv:2610.14617v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LASSO is one of the most popular regularization methods for high-dimensional regression models. While cointegration is common in practical applications of predictive regressions with many regressors, the convex penalty of LASSO overly suppresses the coefficients of cointegrated regressors and therefore fails to deliver consistent parameter estimation. We employ folded concave penalties (FCP), including the well-known SCAD and MCP, to address this issue. Using FCP, we establish two asymptotic results: (i) a local oracle property for the penalized regression, and (ii) a global oracle property for regressions with a penalty-level constraint. In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.
item.dc:creator: Hongqi Chen, Chengwang Liao, Ziwei Mei, Zhentao Shi

item.title: Causal Integrated Gradients: Scalable Feature Attribution Along Causal Paths
item.description: arXiv:2610.22126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing feature attribution methods that account for feature dependencies do not scale to high dimensions. We propose causal integrated gradients (CIG) and causal expected gradients (CEG), which extend integrated gradients to incorporate prior causal structure among input features while retaining its computational efficiency and, under conditions on the causal graph, its axiomatic guarantees. In many settings, some causal structure between features is already known, for example, that a transcription factor causally regulates a target gene's expression. Yet existing gradient-based methods cannot exploit this structure, instead crediting a feature's downstream effects over its true upstream cause, such as ranking the target gene above the transcription factor that regulates it. Our key idea is to embed this causal structure by routing the integration path along the causal graph. The method thereby decomposes each feature's attribution into a direct effect and effects mediated through its causal descendants. We evaluate CIG in three settings of increasing realism. First, on a synthetic benchmark with a known causal model, CIG's attributions best match the ground-truth causal effect from Pearl's do-calculus, matching the accuracy of causal Shapley values at a fraction of the computational cost. Second, on simulated single-cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), CIG most accurately recovers the transcription factors driving the simulation. Third, on real interferon-$\beta$ stimulation data, where only an approximate causal graph is available, CIG better prioritizes the transcription factors driving the measured response than DeepSHAP and integrated gradients. Together, these results show that incorporating causal structure into gradient-based attributions recovers upstream drivers that existing methods miss, without sacrificing scalability.
item.dc:creator: Joran Michiels, Anis Ismail, Maarten De Vos, Alejandro Sifrim

item.title: Upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in spiking neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.22484v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The input space of single-spike neural networks decomposes into causal pieces, and the number of causal pieces has been shown to provide a lower bound on the approximation error for some spiking neural networks. While this decomposition is applicable to a wide range of spiking neuron models, the limits of how many causal pieces can be realised by spiking neural networks are still unknown. In this work, we derive two complementary upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in feedforward single-spike neural networks. First, we establish a combinatorial bound given by the poly-Bernoulli numbers, which applies to a broad class of spiking neuron models. The bound is of order $e^{2(L-1)N\log N+\mathcal{O}(N)}$, with network depth $L$ and maximum layer width $N$. Second, for a specific set of neuron models, we derive a bound based on hyperplane arrangements. Applying the latter framework, we obtain bounds of order $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{(4L-3)(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with exponential synapses and the ReLU-type spike response model, and $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{L(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$\delta$ synapses, where $N_0$ is the input dimension. For the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$\delta$ synapses, additional temporal structure allows us to sharpen the general combinatorial bound to one that depends only on $N_0$, independently of the network depth and widths.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Dold, Dennis Elbr\"achter, Philipp Petersen

item.title: Learning smooth dynamics via Kinematic Interpolants
item.description: arXiv:2610.22519v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Inferring dynamics from real-world experimental data is inherently ambiguous, as many plausible dynamical systems can explain the same positional observations at measurement times. For higher fidelity modeling of applications ranging from single-cell RNA to vortex dynamics and even flocking of birds, scientific observables increasingly also include velocity estimates that serve to resolve this issue. However, incorporating this rich information in a scalable manner, free of simulation or unnecessary approximations, has remained a difficult challenge. In this paper, we introduce Kinematic Interpolants (KI), a novel framework that extends the seminal methodology of stochastic interpolants to infer nonlinear dynamics across multiple snapshots in phase space, i.e., observables with position and velocity measurements. Empirically, we demonstrate that across several scientific datasets, KI achieves superior reconstruction of the underlying dynamics compared to existing baselines while requiring only a fraction of the training time.
item.dc:creator: Yiheng (Roger), Jiang, Youssef Marzouk, Avishek Joey Bose, Aram-Alexandre Pooladian

item.title: Computing Fr\'echet on Unknown Submanifolds of Riemannian Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2610.22592v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Empirical averages are fundamental statistical primitives. On nonlinear spaces, their generalization, the Fr\'echet mean, generally lacks a closed-form solution, and its computation requires solving an optimization problem. We study the computation of intrinsic Fr\'echet means for data supported on an unknown compact $d$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $M_{1}$ embedded in an ambient metric space $(X,d_{\operatorname{obs}})$. Such settings arise when observations are better represented in non-Euclidean spaces, like probability distributions in Wasserstein space. We assume access only to a local sampler on $M_{1}$ and the observation metric $d_{\operatorname{obs}}$, without knowledge of its intrinsic geometry. We propose a graph-based iterative algorithm that adaptively samples the manifold and approximates geodesic interpolation. Under mild assumptions, we establish an $O(1/T)$ expected objective gap guarantee using at most $\widetilde{O}(T^{4d+3})$ sampled points. As a byproduct of our analysis we extend the metric equivalence guarantees of ISOMAP from Euclidean to Riemannian ambient spaces, which may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for computing intrinsic averages on unknown data manifolds.
item.dc:creator: Ian McPherson, Mauro Maggioni

item.title: Flat Loss, Evolving Features: Grokking in Modular Addition
item.description: arXiv:2610.22593v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a network keep learning while its training cross-entropy stays nearly flat at a positive level? We show that it can. On modular addition, a standard testbed for grokking, ReLU networks trained with supported-Polar hidden updates, normalized output-layer updates and weight decay can keep 100% training accuracy while their hidden features change and held-out accuracy rises from zero to above 90%, at relatively flat training cross-entropy. Correct classification need not minimize cross-entropy, which still depends on prediction confidence. We prove this coexistence for one-hidden-layer networks in two finite-window theorems from constructed initializations: one gives a constant gain in the Fourier fraction of the hidden features, and the other holds at arbitrarily low positive loss, where a readout refitted on the training data generalizes before the network. Experiments from random initialization show the same coexistence on a window fixed in advance, and in deeper networks held-out accuracy also rises over post-hoc windows with a net increase in training cross-entropy. With a last-layer rate set per training fraction and head decay scaled with the prime, deeper networks at p=47 and 61 meet a criterion on post-hoc windows, fixed in advance, in nearly all fresh runs. A one-block transformer trained with the same updates and a slowly decaying output gain keeps every training pair correct at every logged checkpoint while its training cross-entropy rises and its held-out accuracy approaches one; with two blocks this holds through the held-out rise, after which training pairs begin to flip. A plateau in training loss need not be a plateau in learning. Code: https://github.com/akashkumar-d/flat-loss-evolving-features.
item.dc:creator: Akash Kumar, Karthik Sankaranarayanan

item.title: Conformal Policy Selection: When to Deploy AI Decisions for Targeted Intervention
item.description: arXiv:2610.22930v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.
item.dc:creator: Junyu Cao, Ruijiang Gao, Maytal Saar-Tsechansky, Mingzhang Yin

item.title: Towards Hyperparameter Transfer for Differentially Private Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.22976v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scaling laws and hyperparameter tuning remain central challenges in training large-scale models, particularly under differential privacy (DP), where optimization is further complicated by noise injection and per-sample gradient clipping. While Maximal Update Parametrization ($\mu$P) allows for zero-shot hyperparameter transfer in standard training, we show that it fails under DP constraints due to the distinct spectral properties of high-dimensional noise versus low-rank gradients. In this work, we introduce DP-$\mu$P, a theoretically grounded framework that extends $\mu$P to the privacy-preserving setting. By analyzing the interaction between gradient clipping, noise injection, and feature learning, we derive a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) condition that governs layer-wise learning rate scaling. Combining this with our proposed spectral scaling formulation, we provide specific scaling rules for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon optimizers. Empirically, we demonstrate that DP-$\mu$P enables effective zero-shot transfer of learning rates across model widths on diverse architectures (MLP, ViT, GPT-2), matching or exceeding the performance of individually tuned baselines while significantly reducing computational costs.
item.dc:creator: Tianze Wang, Zhiqi Bu, Linjun Zhang

item.title: A Class of R\'enyi-based Concentration Metrics for Kolmogorov-Arnold Geometry in Multilayer Perceptrons
item.description: arXiv:2610.23267v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The interpretability of artificial intelligence models has become a central concern, especially for black-box models such as multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Kolmogorov-Arnold Geometry has recently emerged as a framework for analysing the internal representations of these networks, by examining how the hidden layer locally responds to changes in the input through the minors of its Jacobian. The degree to which a few of these minors dominate the rest, known as their concentration, has so far been measured with the Participation Ratio. Although this metric has useful properties, its maximum value depends on the size of the network, so a given value cannot be read as high or low concentration without reference to the architecture. To overcome this limitation, in this paper we propose the $\alpha$-RC metrics, a family of R\'enyi-based concentration measures that compare the normalized magnitudes of the minors with the uniform distribution through the R\'enyi divergence of order $\alpha$. All the metrics in the family are bounded between 0 and 1 regardless of the architecture, with 0 indicating that the magnitude is evenly spread over the minors and 1 that it is carried by a single one. Moreover, the metrics are non-decreasing in $\alpha$, and for $\alpha$ = 2 they reduce to an explicit transformation of the Participation Ratio. Computational experiments with single-hidden-layer MLPs trained on a synthetic dataset show the benefits of our proposal.
item.dc:creator: Juan Carlos Fern\'andez, Asunci\'on Jim\'enez-Cordero, Jos\'e Francisco Paris

item.title: Minimax-optimal Scaling Laws in Ridge Regression via Transfer Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.23337v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pretrained models are often reused across downstream tasks, motivating the question of whether this transfer learning procedure can provide a substantial performance improvement, namely, in terms of the scaling law. We address this question in the prototypical setting of high-dimensional regression, where (i) a pretrained \emph{source} model is trained via ridge regression, and (ii) a fine-tuned \emph{target} model is regularized via the $L_2$ distance from the source estimator. First, we establish a deterministic equivalent for the risk of this two-step procedure under both model and covariance shift. Next, by specializing the deterministic equivalent to a shared regression function and commuting power-law covariance spectra, we identify a regime where the resulting scaling law achieves the minimax-optimal exponent. Notably, in this regime, the optimal source regularization depends on source data only, indicating its universality across all targets. Furthermore, we show that the same optimal rate is achieved by performing the fine-tuning step via one-pass stochastic gradient descent. We support our theoretical analysis via experiments on both synthetic settings and language models.
item.dc:creator: Yalda Shabanzadeh, Diyuan Wu, Marco Mondelli

item.title: Causal Discovery beyond Conditional Independence: Identifiability, Algorithms, and Statistical Inference for Directed Acyclic and Cyclic Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23543v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning causal structure from data requires assumptions about mechanisms, noises, observation schemes, and interventions. Historically, causal discovery has relied primarily on conditional independence. This review focuses on modern causal discovery methods that exploit properties of distributions beyond conditional independence. Our organizing principle separates the source of identification from the statistical estimator and its computational implementation. This perspective connects conditional-independence methods with distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. We examine discovery under latent confounding and feedback, distinguishing causal information about observed variables from reconstruction of latent structure and emphasizing the additional semantics required by cyclic models. We also distinguish population identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification, and algorithmic guarantees. Throughout, examples show why the same observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes. We conclude with guidance for comparing methods at their identifiable targets and a research agenda for uncertainty, heterogeneous populations, non-scalar variables, and the intersection of discrete data, feedback, and hidden confounding.
item.dc:creator: Yang Ni

item.title: Beyond Expected Values: Risk-Sensitive Planning with Distributional Monte-Carlo Tree Search
item.description: arXiv:2610.23565v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) typically stores only scalar mean estimates, which makes it poorly suited for tail-risk objectives such as conditional value-at-risk (CVaR). We introduce Categorical Thompson Sampling with Optimism (CATSO) and Particle Thompson Sampling with Optimism (PATSO), two distributional MCTS algorithms that maintain finite-support empirical backup laws at Q-edges. CATSO represents Q-edge laws with categorical atoms and Dirichlet Thompson sampling, while PATSO represents them with adaptive particles. Both algorithms select actions using the CVaR of a Thompson-sampled Q-edge law plus a polynomial optimism bonus, and propagate scalar continuation values through visit-weighted averages of child Q-edge CVaR scores. For the finite-depth nested CVaR planning target, we prove an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on the root value error after $n$ rollouts, which upper-bounds the risk-sensitive simple regret. CATSO adds a fixed-grid discretization bias, while capped PATSO adds a tunable Wasserstein compression bias. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show that distributional Q-edges improve lower-tail return and reduce catastrophic outcomes when mean-optimal and risk-sensitive behavior differ.
item.dc:creator: Quynh Trinh, Trung Nguyen, Nam Nguyen, Tuan Dam

item.title: Boundary Detection for High-Dimensional Point Clouds
item.description: arXiv:2610.23590v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce two new methods for boundary detection in high-dimensional point cloud data, intended to work in situations with non-uniform density, high ambient dimension, and substantial noise. Our first method fits a separating hyperplane on local neighborhoods after doing local dimension reduction---this method works best when one can reliably estimate the intrinsic dimension of the data. Our second method measures the directional uniformity of local neighborhoods, and has the best overall performance on synthetic data. In addition to pointwise numerical boundary scores, our algorithms yield an estimated normal vector at each boundary point. We validate our methodology on synthetic data as well as two real examples: we analyze spatial transcriptomics data, where we show that we can detect the boundary of a tumor, and we also study LLM activation geometry.
item.dc:creator: Abigail Hickok, Valerio Galanti, Osama Al Dalahmah, Andrew J. Blumberg

item.title: No-Regret Language Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.23641v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce no-regret generation, which requires a generator to make a sublinear number of mistakes uniformly over all demonstration sequences and compatible target languages. We also formulate an agnostic variant that allows arbitrary demonstrations that may not be compatible with any languages. For both settings, we introduce tree-based mistake-forcing dimensions that exactly characterize finite-horizon minimax complexity and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for no-regret generation. Our characterizations reveal a rich spectrum of generation rates: up to constant rescaling, every admissible nondecreasing profile is attainable in both the realizable and agnostic settings. Finally, we connect generation complexity to online prediction: for language classes of finite Littlestone dimension \(d\), we obtain realizable mistake bounds of \(O(d\log(1+T/d))\) and agnostic regret bounds of \(O(\sqrt{dT\log(1+T/d)})\). The realizable bound is optimal up to universal constants.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxun Li, Vinod Raman, Ambuj Tewari

item.title: Equivalence testing and run-count design for stochastic machine-learning experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.23700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Claims that two training methods perform equally well often rest on a non-significant difference between two or three runs per method. We develop a protocol, with its power theory, for certifying practical equivalence in per-run metrics such as the AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). It rests on a two-level (seed x item) variance model separating between-run dispersion from item-level noise. Equivalence within a pre-specified margin is tested by two one-sided tests (TOST), equivalently by a confidence interval inside the margin; a two-level bootstrap covers composite statistics. A closed-form formula converts a margin and a target power into runs per method; its shifted-t refinement is calibrated against the realised two-level process. Simulations on a 270-cell grid and under non-Gaussian seed laws confirm the formula within its design-relevant range, from five runs per method. For four published runs of a joint energy-based model, the failure to certify equivalence was largely decided by design: with the variance calibrated to those runs, two per method certify with probability near three per cent, whereas certifying 0.01 AUROC at 80 per cent power needs twelve even under exact equality. A second case study on a thousand-seed CIFAR-10 zoo and the MultiBERTs checks the formula against real seed laws (within 0.05 in that range) and resolves comparisons that two or three runs leave undecided. In a two-stage design (pilot, then formula), our experiments suggest that an upper confidence bound on the pilot variance substantially reduces the undersizing seen with its point estimate.
item.dc:creator: Dmytro Knopov, Nadiya Shvai

item.title: Exact Tail Laws for Nonlinear SGD with Infinite-Variance Gradients
item.description: arXiv:2610.23750v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: With infinite-variance gradient noise, SGD can have infinite expected excess objective even when most iterates are close to the optimum. We characterize its accuracy through exact first-order tail probabilities for the last iterate of nonlinear, constant-stepsize SGD. For regularly varying innovations of index $t\in(1,2)$, the leading measure transports one large gradient shock through the local Hessian flow. This is the same measure that governs the central stable Ornstein--Uhlenbeck limit; we prove its relative accuracy at shrinking tolerances above the central scale, with state-dependent noise and a growing observation horizon. The admissible window is nonempty for every available gradient moment $p>1$. The main technical step is a moment bound at the central fluctuation scale and a lower-moment control of the nonlinear error. The result yields explicit projection and excess-objective tails, extreme quantiles, and a factor $b^{1-t}$ for fixed batch size $b$. For affine population gradients, a sharper comparison gives the same law at fixed tolerances, including random sample Hessians. Coupled simulations in dimensions one to one hundred examine relative calibration, objective quantiles, batch effects, and the error due to random curvature.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoli Li, Qianqian Lei, Ziyang Wei, Wei Biao Wu

item.title: Deep conditional distribution learning via conditional F\"ollmer flow
item.description: arXiv:2402.01460v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce an ordinary differential equation (ODE) based deep generative method for learning conditional distributions, named Conditional F\"ollmer Flow. Starting from a standard Gaussian distribution, the proposed flow could approximate the target conditional distribution very well when the time is close to 1. For effective implementation, we discretize the flow with Euler's method where we estimate the velocity field nonparametrically using a deep neural network. Furthermore, we also establish the convergence result for the Wasserstein-2 distance between the distribution of the learned samples and the target conditional distribution, providing the first comprehensive end-to-end error analysis for conditional distribution learning via ODE flow. Our numerical experiments showcase its effectiveness across a range of scenarios, from standard nonparametric conditional density estimation problems to more intricate challenges involving image data, illustrating its superiority over various existing conditional density estimation methods.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Zhao Ding, Yuling Jiao, Ruoxuan Li, Jerry Zhijian Yang

item.title: What is causal about causal models and representations?
item.description: arXiv:2501.19335v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal Bayesian networks are often described as causal because they support reasoning about interventions. Yet interventions are defined in the mathematical model, whereas the resulting model predictions concern the effects of actions in the real world. Consequently, whether and how a causal model makes falsifiable predictions about the effects of actions depends on how actions are interpreted as interventions. This requires specifying which actions correspond to which interventions, a step that is frequently left implicit. We develop a formal framework that separates a causal model from the data-generating process it aims to describe and formalizes interpretations connecting actions to interventions. Within this framework, we prove an impossibility result: no interpretation can simultaneously satisfy a collection of desirable properties while remaining non-circular. Under a circular interpretation, every model that fits the observational distribution is interventionally valid, so no experiment can falsify it. We analyze several non-circular alternatives and discuss implications for falsification, causal discovery, causal representation learning, and causal abstraction. More broadly, our framework provides a way to make assumptions about the connections between actions and interventions explicit and to reason formally about the empirical content of causal models.
item.dc:creator: Frederik Hytting J{\o}rgensen, Luigi Gresele, Sebastian Weichwald

item.title: Optimal estimates for the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants of deep random ReLU neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2506.19695v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants of ReLU neural networks $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ with random parameters for $p \in [1,\infty]$. The distribution of the weights follows a variant of the He initialization. In the case of zero-bias networks, we derive matching high-probability upper and lower bounds for wide networks that differ at most by an absolute constant. The bounds reveal two remarkable phenomena. First, the bounds grow root-logarithmically in terms of the depth of the net. Second, the behavior of the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants varies significantly between the regimes $p \in [1,2)$ and $p \in [2,\infty]$. For $p \in [2,\infty]$, the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constant behaves similarly to $\|g\|_{p'}$, where $g \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a standard Gaussian vector and $1/p + 1/p' = 1$. In contrast, for $p \in [1,2)$, the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constant aligns more closely with $\|g\|_2$. For networks with possibly nonzero biases, we obtain the same lower bounds without assumptions on the bias distributions. For symmetric bias distributions with bounded densities, we also derive high-probability upper bounds for the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants. For fixed sub-exponential bias distributions, these upper bounds differ from the lower bounds by a factor that has square-root dependence on the depth and logarithmic dependence on the width.
item.dc:creator: Sjoerd Dirksen, Patrick Finke, Paul Geuchen, Dominik St\"oger, Felix Voigtlaender

item.title: Missing value imputation with adversarial random forests - MissARF
item.description: arXiv:2507.15681v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Handling missing values is a common challenge in biostatistical analyses, typically addressed by imputation methods. We propose a novel, fast, and easy-to-use imputation method called missing value imputation with adversarial random forests (MissARF), based on generative machine learning, that provides both single and multiple imputation. MissARF employs adversarial random forest (ARF) for density estimation and data synthesis. To impute a missing value of an observation, we condition on the non-missing values and sample from the estimated conditional distribution generated by ARF. Our experiments demonstrate that MissARF performs comparably to state-of-the-art single and multiple imputation methods in terms of imputation quality and fast runtime with no additional costs for multiple imputation.
item.dc:creator: Pegah Golchian, Jan Kapar, David S. Watson, Marvin N. Wright

item.title: Reinforcement Learning in MDPs with Information-Ordered Policies
item.description: arXiv:2508.03904v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many operational Markov decision processes provide structured information where a trajectory generated under one policy may also reveal how other policies would have performed. We formalize this through an information order over a parameterized policy class, writing $\pi_{\theta'} \preceq \pi_\theta$ when data collected under $\pi_\theta$ can be used to estimate the long-run average cost of $\pi_{\theta'}$. We develop an epoch-based reinforcement learning algorithm for infinite-horizon average-cost MDPs with continuous state and action spaces that exploits this order through counterfactual inference. For a $d$-dimensional policy class whose information order has width $w$, the algorithm achieves $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{wdT/\alpha})$ regret relative to the optimal policy in the class, where $H$ is a bias span upper bound and $\alpha$ denotes an "information ratio". Thus, the width captures the effective exploration complexity of the problem, interpolating between full counterfactual feedback and unstructured policy learning. We instantiate the framework in lost-sales inventory systems with positive lead times, dual-sourcing systems governed by dual-index policies, and queues with state-dependent service rates. These applications yield new regret guarantees without requiring global convexity of the average-cost function or specialized arrival-rate structure. Numerical experiments show that exploiting the information order substantially improves learning performance over existing general-purpose and problem-specific benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Zhongjun Zhang, Shipra Agrawal, Ilan Lobel, Sean R. Sinclair, Christina Lee Yu

item.title: The Statistical Fairness-Accuracy Frontier
item.description: arXiv:2508.17622v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study fairness-accuracy tradeoffs when a single predictive model must serve multiple demographic groups. A useful tool for understanding this tradeoff is the fairness-accuracy (FA) Pareto frontier, which characterizes the set of models that cannot be improved in either fairness or accuracy without worsening the other. While characterizing the FA frontier requires full knowledge of the data distribution, we focus on the finite-sample regime, quantifying how well a designer can approximate any point on the frontier from limited data and bounding the worst-case gap. In particular, we derive worst-case-optimal estimators that depend on the designer's knowledge of the covariate distribution. For each estimator, we characterize how finite-sample effects asymmetrically impact each group's welfare and identify optimal sample allocation strategies. Finally, we provide uniform finite-sample bounds along the entire FA frontier, quantifying finite-sample deviations across alternative fairness-accuracy tradeoffs.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Fallah, Michael I. Jordan, Annie Ulichney

item.title: Reliable data clustering with Bayesian community detection
item.description: arXiv:2510.15013v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: From neuroscience and genomics to systems biology and ecology, researchers rely on clustering similarity data to uncover modular structure. Most methods work in two steps: first reduce noise, then cluster. The first step runs without regard to the second: it forces arbitrary choices, discards useful information, and can impose structure where none exists. Here we bring the two steps together. Using established Bayesian community detection methods, we let one minimum description length criterion choose both how much to sparsify the data and how to cluster it. This one-step approach keeps all the samples for inference, removes the arbitrary threshold choice, and returns a single cluster when there is no real structure. On synthetic data, our approach recovers clusters under more noise and with fewer samples than standard methods. On gene co-expression data from the human brain, it finds more coherent and more stable clusters than WGCNA, the standard tool in the field. Uniting sparsification and clustering in a single model-selection step provides a principled, noise-resistant way to uncover modular structure in similarity data across fields.
item.dc:creator: Magnus Neuman, Jelena Smiljani\'c, Martin Rosvall

item.title: Robust Experimental Design via Generalised Bayesian Inference
item.description: arXiv:2511.07671v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian optimal experimental design is a principled framework for conducting experiments that leverages Bayesian inference to quantify how much information one can expect to gain from selecting a certain design. However, accurate Bayesian inference relies on the assumption that one's statistical model of the data-generating process is correctly specified. If this assumption is violated, Bayesian methods can lead to poor inference and estimates of information gain. Generalised Bayesian (or Gibbs) inference is a more robust probabilistic inference framework that replaces the likelihood in the Bayesian update by a suitable loss function. In this work, we present Generalised Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design (GBOED), an extension of generalised Bayesian inference to the experimental design setting which achieves robustness in both design and inference. Using a generalisation of Bayesian decision theory, we derive a new acquisition function, the Gibbs expected information gain. Our empirical results demonstrate that GBOED can enhance robustness to outliers and incorrect assumptions about the outcome noise distribution.
item.dc:creator: Yasir Zubayr Barlas, Sabina J. Sloman, Samuel Kaski

item.title: Structural Causal Bottleneck Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.08682v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce structural causal bottleneck models (SCBMs), a novel class of structural causal models in which causal effects between high-dimensional variables are mediated by low-dimensional summary statistics, or *bottlenecks*. SCBMs provide a flexible framework for mechanism-specific, target-dependent dimension reduction while remaining estimable via standard learning algorithms. We prove that bottleneck variables are identifiable up to bijection from observational data, and validate this experimentally. We then study causal effect estimation in linear SCBMs under three standard adjustment strategies. For instrumental variables, we identify a population-level non-identifiability of na\"ive two-stage least squares when all variables are high-dimensional, and show that bottleneck representations restore identification. For mediation and backdoor adjustment, we prove that conditioning on bottleneck variables yields valid effect estimates with explicit finite-sample efficiency gains over conditioning on full high-dimensional variables. We argue that SCBMs provide a principled alternative to existing causal dimension reduction frameworks such as causal representation learning and causal abstractions.
item.dc:creator: Simon Bing, Jonas Wahl, Jakob Runge

item.title: Measuring Differences between Conditional Distributions using Kernel Embeddings
item.description: arXiv:2605.02260v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Comparing conditional distributions is a fundamental challenge in statistics and machine learning, with applications across a wide range of domains. While proposed methods for measuring discrepancies using kernel embeddings of distributions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) provide powerful non-parametric techniques, the existing literature remains fragmented and lacks a unified theoretical treatment. This paper addresses this gap by establishing a coherent framework for studying kernel-based methods to measure divergence between conditional distributions through what we refer to as conditional maximum mean discrepancy (CMMD). The CMMD consists of a family of metrics which we call levels, with three special cases each using a different type of RKHS embedding: CMMD$_0$ (conditional mean operators), CMMD$_1$ (conditional mean embeddings), and CMMD$_2$ (joint mean embeddings). We additionally introduce a general level $s$ CMMD, clarifying the required assumptions, and establishing mathematical connections between the levels through the lens of operator-based smoothing. In addition to reviewing previously proposed estimators, we introduce a novel doubly robust estimator for the CMMD that maintains consistency provided the product of errors of the underlying models reduces sufficiently fast. We provide numerical experiments demonstrating that the CMMD effectively captures complex conditional dependencies for statistical testing.
item.dc:creator: Peter Moskvichev, Siu Lun Chau, Dino Sejdinovic

item.title: Diffusion-Based Stochastic Operator Networks for Uncertainty Quantification in Stochastic Partial Differential Equations
item.description: arXiv:2605.17107v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a novel framework for uncertainty quantification of solution operators associated with stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs). Although SPDEs play a central role in modeling complex physical systems under uncertainty, their practical use typically requires specifying the magnitude and structure of model uncertainties that are often unknown and difficult to infer from noisy measurements. To address this challenge, we develop a stochastic operator-learning framework that learns directly from noisy data and outputs both a mean solution field and a quantification of uncertainty. The proposed method, namely the Stochastic Operator Network (SON), is constructed by combining the structure of the Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) with Stochastic Neural Networks (SNNs) to model stochasticity and enable probabilistic prediction. The training procedure is carried out by minimizing a Hamiltonian-type loss and optimizing the resulting objective using the Stochastic Maximum Principle. Numerical experiments on benchmark SPDEs under multiple uncertainty sources demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the proposed method in capturing solution structure and quantifying predictive uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Phuoc-Toan Huynh, Richard Archibald, Feng Bao

item.title: Dynamics of Stochastic Momentum with Sparse Updates in High Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2605.28961v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing theory of momentum assumes that gradients arrive at every parameter at a roughly constant rate, an assumption violated in practice by heavy-tailed data distributions and modern architectures. We theoretically analyze the dynamics of two tractable models of momentum under sparse updates: a least squares model with sparse inputs and a logistic regression model with a rare class. Both admit exact closed-form second-moment dynamics whose high-dimensional limits we characterize across three scaling exponents for sparsity, batch size, and momentum decay. The phase structure on both problems is governed by the ratio of two intrinsic timescales: a momentum retention timescale (how many active updates the buffer survives) and a learning timescale (how many active updates it takes to reduce the squared error). When learning is much slower than retention, the limit matches SGD; when learning is faster, the system is unstable; where the timescales coincide, we recover classical heavy-ball dynamics. The oscillatory dynamics occur at different momentum values for different token sparsity, creating a spectral conflict for global momentum across token frequencies.
item.dc:creator: Katie Everett, Elliot Paquette

item.title: Online Inference for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.12973v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study online statistical inference for quantile-based distributional policy evaluation, which aims to characterize the distribution of discounted cumulative rewards under a given policy. To obtain a finite-dimensional representation of the return distribution, we consider the fixed point $\bm\eta_m$ of the quantile-projected distributional Bellman equation, parameterized by the quantile vector $\bm\theta_m$. We develop two online inference procedures for $\bm\theta_m$, covering synchronous and asynchronous sampling from a generative model as well as Markovian data. The first method uses the trajectory of quantile temporal-difference learning (QTD). We establish functional central limit theorems for the partial sums of QTD iterates and construct a recursively computable random-scaling statistic. The resulting confidence intervals have asymptotically exact coverage at deterministic horizons, with length of order $T^{-1/2}$ in probability. The second method constructs anytime-valid confidence intervals directly from samples. Exploiting the monotonicity of the quantile Bellman map, we develop a computationally explicit coordinate-shaving algorithm with finite-sample simultaneous coverage. Under positive limiting state-visit frequencies, the resulting confidence intervals have lengths of order $\sqrt{\log\log T/T}$, which we establish as classwise optimal through a matching lower bound. Together, these results provide complementary guarantees for online inference in quantile distributional reinforcement learning, combining asymptotically exact fixed-horizon inference with finite-sample anytime validity.
item.dc:creator: Zijie Cheng, Yang Peng, Zhihua Zhang

item.title: Online Inference in Distributional Temporal-Difference Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.14408v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online statistical inference for functionals of the return distribution under a fixed policy. The return distribution is estimated by nonparametric distributional temporal-difference learning from a single Markov trajectory. For the Polyak--Ruppert averaged estimator, we prove that its root-$T$ error converges weakly to a centered Gaussian random element in Cram\'er space. We also prove that, conditionally on the observed trajectory, the root-$T$ difference between the bootstrap and original averages converges weakly to the same Gaussian limit. These results justify bootstrap inference for smooth statistical functionals, including variance, CVaR, expected shortfall, and expectiles. For nonsmooth statistical functionals, we develop a local asymptotic theory for the estimated return CDF over $T^{-1/2}$-neighborhoods of finitely many thresholds, together with its bootstrap analogue. This theory allows us to conduct inference for nonsmooth statistical functionals characterized by CDF equations, including return quantiles.
item.dc:creator: Yang Peng, Liangyu Zhang

item.title: On the Sample Complexity of Active Learning with Membership Queries
item.description: arXiv:2609.27241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work revisits a fundamental question in active learning: how powerful is the ability to synthesize arbitrary queries? Compared to pool-based active learning, where the learner only selects queries from a given unlabeled pool, it has been observed that this seemingly mild change in query ability may dramatically alter the difficulty of statistical learning. In particular some hypothesis classes, such as two dimensional halfspaces, permit only polynomial error decay in the number of samples when the learner must draw its labels from the pool, yet become exponentially learnable once synthesized queries are allowed. This striking gap suggests that membership query synthesis induces a fundamentally different mode of learning, one that is not adequately captured by existing active learning theory and calls for new analytical tools to characterize its sample complexity for general hypothesis classes. Motivated by this phenomenon, we develop several sufficient conditions, present intriguing examples, and propose a conjectural perspective toward understanding which hypothesis classes admit efficient learning through synthesized queries.
item.dc:creator: Ganghua Wang, Shaddin Dughmi

item.title: The optimal information complexity of VC learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.10600v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Steinke and Zakynthinou(2020) introduces the Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) framework of analyzing the information complexity of learning algorithms based on algorithm-dependent information-theoretic quantities. We study one of these quantities, the evaluated Conditional Mutual Information (eCMI). It has been an interesting question whether the optimal PAC guarantee for VC classes can be recovered from the algorithm-dependent analyses via CMI. And we show that it is possible to recover this guarantee by constructing a learning algorithm whose eCMI is of order O(d) in the realizable case, where d is the VC-dimension of the concept class. Specially, our algorithm is a randomized Majority-of-5 base learners with optimal in-expectation generalization guarantee.
item.dc:creator: Steve Hanneke, Juexiao Wang

item.title: How Well Do Prior-Data Fitted Networks Amortize Bayesian Inference?
item.description: arXiv:2610.13764v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are trained to approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution (PPD) of a synthetic prior, yet results about the approximation quality are surprisingly thin. Taking an empirical risk minimization perspective, we decompose the deployment error of PFNs into prior, context, and amortization error, and measure the latter against a reference PPD under a realistic prior. Results show that PFNs generally recover the targeted PPD very well. Nevertheless, we find that parts of the residual amortization error persist, especially in \textit{rare} settings under the prior pretraining distribution, even when scaling the model size, which manifests in disagreement between independently pretrained PFNs and leaves uncertainty about the predictor at inference time. As a remedy, we study multiple types of Bayesian model averages and find that these can consistently reduce this uncertainty and improve predictions up to full-size TabICLv2 models.
item.dc:creator: Manuel H\"ulskamp, Julius Kobialka, Emanuel Sommer, Thomas Nagler, David R\"ugamer

item.title: Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.20860v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nonstationarity and heterogeneous dynamics are common in financial and macroeconomic time series. Volatility alternates between calm and turbulent regimes, interest rates follow monetary-policy cycles, and major events trigger persistent structural shifts. We propose the Time-partitioning Gaussian Process Mixture Model (TPGPMM), a Bayesian nonparametric framework for regime identification and nonstationary prediction that infers such regimes and their within-regime dependence from data, without Markovian assumptions. It combines (i) an adaptive Pitman-Yor process prior on ordered compositions, mapped to block lengths with contiguity enforced by construction, and (ii) regime-specific Gaussian processes for temporal dependence, yielding a nonstationary predictive distribution. By inferring its discount parameter, the prior adapts to homogeneous and highly heterogeneous regime lengths. Unlike sequential or Markov-switching methods, it flags persistent structural shifts as change points rather than reacting to transient shocks. A split-merge Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with exact Gibbs updates of regime boundaries jointly learns change points and hyperparameters in batch, quantifying uncertainty over the partition and within-regime dynamics. With an RBF kernel and a fixed, data-informed noise level, TPGPMM produces a sparse, confident segmentation. On simulated data it recovers the true regimes, and on the CBOE Volatility Index and the 10-year US Treasury yield it identifies regimes aligned with documented market and monetary-policy events. For prediction, variants estimating the noise level fit better than change-point baselines and fit and forecast better than the main specification, at the cost of a less sparse or less event-aligned segmentation; with a regime mean, they fit better than a fitted stationary Gaussian process and have lower forecast RMSE except at the shortest horizons.
item.dc:creator: Guilherme Piantino, Hedibert F. Lopes

item.title: Is the Policy Gradient a Gradient?
item.description: arXiv:1906.07073v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The policy gradient theorem describes the gradient of the expected discounted return with respect to an agent's policy parameters. However, many policy gradient methods omit the outer discount factor, yielding an update that need not equal the gradient of the discounted objective. Is the resulting update the gradient of another objective? This has been an open question for several years, and this lack of theoretical clarity has led to an abundance of misstatements in the literature. We answer this question for the resulting episode-summed, on-policy update by proving that it need not equal the gradient of any function. Further, we construct a counterexample in which exact expected updates drive the policy toward a deterministic limit that is globally pessimal with respect to both the discounted and undiscounted objectives, while the parameter diverges. We motivate this work by surveying the literature and showing that there remains a widespread misunderstanding regarding discounted policy gradient methods, with errors present even in highly-cited papers published at top conferences.
item.dc:creator: Chris Nota, Philip S. Thomas

item.title: RAW-Explainer: Post-hoc Explanations of Path Reasoning Graph Neural Networks for Knowledge Graph Completion
item.description: arXiv:2506.12558v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Path reasoning graph neural networks have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on knowledge graph completion tasks such as link prediction. However, interpreting their predictions remains a challenging open problem, as most GNN explainability methods target node-level or graph-level tasks. In this paper, we propose RAW-Explainer ($\underline{Ra}$ndom $\underline{W}$alk Explainer), a novel explainability method tailored to path reasoning GNNs that generates connected, concise, and interpretable subgraph explanations for link prediction in knowledge graphs. Our method uses heterogeneous information to identify factual explanations and encourages connectivity through a random walk objective, using a parameterized model for efficient collective explanation. Furthermore, RAW-Explainer overcomes the distribution shift issue when evaluating explanatory subgraphs that are orders of magnitude smaller than the full graph by proposing a robust evaluator that generalizes to the subgraph distribution. Extensive results on standard knowledge graph completion benchmarks demonstrate that our approach strikes a balance between explanation quality and computational efficiency. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/colab-nyuad/RAWExplainer
item.dc:creator: Ryoji Kubo, Samyam Lamichhane, Djellel Difallah

item.title: Closed-form Covariance Functions in Space and Time from B-spline Spectral Densities
item.description: arXiv:2506.21953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The autocovariance function (ACF) is central to the analysis of time series, spatial, and spatio-temporal data. Classical parametric models are often too restrictive for multivariate and space-time data, which motivates non-parametric descriptions of the ACF. Bochner's Theorem guarantees that any positive spectral measure yields a valid ACF via the inverse Fourier transform; however, existing non-parametric approaches in the spectral domain rarely return closed-form expressions for the ACF itself. We develop a closed-form class of non-parametric ACFs by deriving the inverse Fourier transform of B-spline spectral bases with arbitrary degree and knot placement. This yields a family of closed-form stationary covariance models with three properties: (i) it is uniformly dense for the ACF, among the ACFs of weakly stationary processes that possess a spectral density; (ii) it accommodates univariate, multivariate, and multidimensional processes; and (iii) it is non-separable in general, with separability a special case. Jackson-type approximation bounds establish convergence rates, and simulation studies show accurate recovery of known univariate and bivariate ACFs.
